description: We built a lunar south-pole landing-site navigator scoring candidate sites on solar power and Earth comms visibility across the 2026-2027 window, using live NASA Horizons ephemeris data
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator lets mission planners, educators and the public compare candidate lunar south-polar landing sites and dates in seconds. For four Artemis-era candidate sites (Shackleton Rim, de Gerlache Rim, Malapert Massif, Amundsen Rim) it shows when the Sun is above the horizon for solar power and when Earth is above the horizon for direct-to-Earth communication. Every value comes from the NASA/JPL Horizons API with the observer pinned to each site on the lunar surface: 601 samples per target at a 6-hour step from November 2026 to March 2027. Users pick a date window and a Sun mask angle, and each site's power percentage, comms percentage and combined score update instantly, with an elevation chart and CSV export. Over this window no site wins both: Shackleton has the most sunlight (71.2%) while Amundsen keeps Earth in view longest (80.7%). That trade-off is what a landing-site decision has to weigh, and the tool puts it on one screen.
details: What it doesFor any of four candidate lunar south-polar landing sites and any date window, the tool shows when the Sun is above the horizon (solar power for landers, habitats and rovers) and when Earth is above the horizon (direct-to-Earth communication). Each site gets a power percentage, a comms percentage and a combined score, so sites can be ranked at a glance. Selecting a site draws Sun and Earth elevation against the horizon across the whole window, and CSV export hands planners every underlying sample.How it worksWe query the NASA/JPL Horizons API with a body-fixed observer on the Moon (CENTER='coord@301' with selenographic SITE_COORD for each site). Quantity 4 returns the apparent azimuth and elevation of the Sun (COMMAND 10) and Earth (COMMAND 399), corrected for light-time, stellar aberration, precession and nutation in an airless frame. The bundled dataset covers 2026-11-01 to 2027-03-31 at a 6-hour step: 4 sites x 2 targets x 601 samples. A small stdlib-only Python script (scripts/fetch_ephemeris.py) regenerates it with no API key. The web app is static HTML, CSS and JavaScript with a hand-built SVG chart, so it loads instantly and runs on GitHub Pages.What the data showsOver this window no single site wins both. Shackleton Rim has the most sunlight (Sun up 71.2% of the time) but Earth is up only 42.3%. Amundsen Rim keeps Earth in view 80.7% of the time with 50.9% sunlight and the best combined score (0.643). Malapert Massif balances the two (54.4% / 64.4%). Raising the Sun mask angle to model panel height or local terrain changes the ranking, which the tool shows immediately.Why it mattersSouth-polar missions live on the narrow margins where the Sun and Earth skim the horizon. Horizons has the answer but is built for specialists. This tool turns it into a side-by-side comparison that a mission planner, a teacher or a curious member of the public can read in seconds.Next stepsMask the horizon with LOLA terrain so crater walls and ridges count, add more candidate sites, and add mission-specific thresholds for power and link budgets.Tools: Python 3 (stdlib), JavaScript, SVG, GitHub Pages, NASA/JPL Horizons API.
